abstract: Emergence agitation (EA) and emergence delirium (ED) are significant postoperative complications in pediatric anesthesia, requiring effective strategies for prevention and management. This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of intranasal dexmedetomidine, intravenous propofol, and their combination in reducing the incidence and severity of EA/ED in pediatric patients undergoing dental procedures under general anesthesia. In this randomized, controlled trial, 166 pediatric patients were randomized into three groups: intranasal dexmedetomidine (Group Dex), IV propofol (Group Propofol), or a combination of both (Group Dexofol; 0.5 μg.kg-1 dexmedetomidine and 0.5 mg.kg-1 propofol). The primary outcome was EA/ED severity, assessed using PAED scores at 5, 10, and 15 minutes after extubation. EA/ED incidence was analyzed as a secondary outcome and was defined as a PAED score ≥10 at any assessment during the first 15 minutes after extubation. The incidence of EA/ED was lower in the Dex group (21.8%; relative risk [RR] versus the Propofol group, 0.36; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.21-0.61) and the Dexofol group (29.8%; RR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.31-0.77) than in the Propofol group (61.1%). PAED scores at 5 minutes post-extubation were significantly lower in the Dex group, and at 10 minutes were significantly lower in both the Dex and Dexofol groups compared to the Propofol group (p<0.05). Time to PACU discharge readiness was shorter in the Dex group (13.1 ± 2.7 minutes) and the Dexofol group (14.0 ± 3.4 minutes) than in the Propofol group (17.5 ± 4.4 minutes; both p<0.001). Intranasal dexmedetomidine was associated with a lower incidence and severity of EA/ED and earlier achievement of PACU discharge readiness than intravenous propofol. The findings related to the reduced-dose dexmedetomidine-propofol regimen should be regarded as hypothesis-generating, as the study design did not allow differentiation between additive, dose-sparing, and agent-specific effects. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06466915. Prospectively registered on 14 June 2024.

title: Correction: Comment - Louis XIV's terminal illness clinical chronology favors necrotizing soft-tissue infection.
The effects of dexamethasone on the behavior and neurotransmitters of asthmatic model mice.
abstract: Patients with acute asthma frequently present with both neurological and psychological manifestations. Changes in neurotransmitter levels may provide objective indicators for assessing behavioral status. This study was conducted to investigate the effects of dexamethasone on motor behavior, neurotransmitter levels, and inflammatory mediators in a murine asthma model. Dopamine (DA), acetylcholine (ACh), γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and interleukin-4 (IL-4) were measured to assess neuroimmune interactions. Twenty-four C57 mice were randomly assigned to control, asthma, and treatment groups. Mice were initially sensitized with Der p1 and subsequently challenged with house dust mite (HDM) extract. Mice in the treatment group received dexamethasone (1 mg/kg) before challenge, after which motor behavior was evaluated using the open field test. ELISA was used to measure IL-4, TNF-α, GABA, and DA in plasma; IL-4 and TNF-α in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF); and TNF-α, GABA, DA, and ACh in brain tissue. Compared with the asthma group, the treatment group showed significantly reduced IL-4 and TNF-α levels in BALF (all P < 0.05). Plasma GABA and DA levels were increased, whereas plasma IL-4 and TNF-α levels were decreased (all P < 0.05). In brain tissue, ACh and TNF-α levels were decreased, whereas GABA and DA levels were increased (all P < 0.05). In the open field test, the total distance traveled, the proportion of time spent in the central area and speed in the peripheral area of the asthma group were all lower than those of the treatment group, while time spent in the peripheral area was higher than that of the treatment group (all P < 0.05). Correlation analysis showed that IL-4, TNF-α, and brain ACh levels were negatively correlated with total movement distance, time spent in the central area, mean speed in the central area, and mean speed in the peripheral area (all P < 0.05). Plasma DA levels were positively correlated with these behavioral indicators (all P < 0.05). Locomotor and exploratory behavior in asthmatic mice was improved by dexamethasone. The therapeutic effect of dexamethasone on asthma-associated behavioral changes may be associated with concurrent modulation of neurotransmitter levels and suppression of Th cell-related inflammatory mediators.

title: TyG-WC as a composite marker of metabolic dysfunction and central obesity predicts all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in overweight and obese adults.
abstract: Simple and scalable tools for mortality risk stratification in individuals with overweight or obesity remain limited. The triglyceride-glucose-waist circumference (TyG-WC) index integrates insulin resistance and central adiposity, but its prognostic value for mortality in this high-risk population is not well established. We analyzed 11,560 adults with overweight or obesity from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (1999-2018) with mortality follow-up through 2019. Associations between TyG-WC and all-cause and cardiovascular mortality were assessed using multivariable Cox proportional hazards models and restricted cubic spline analyses. Subgroup, exploratory mediation, and sensitivity analyses, including propensity score matching and competing risk models, were performed. Over a median follow-up of 7.6 years, 1,098 deaths occurred, including 294 from cardiovascular disease. Compared with participants in the lowest TyG-WC quartile (Q1), those in the highest quartile (Q4) had significantly higher risks of all-cause mortality (HR 1.589, 95% CI 1.308-1.929) and cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.728, 95% CI 1.158-2.579). When analyzed as a continuous variable, higher TyG-WC levels were also independently associated with increased risks of all-cause mortality (adjusted HR 1.135, 95% CI 1.063-1.211) and cardiovascular mortality (adjusted HR 1.168, 95% CI 1.031-1.324). The associations showed an overall positive dose-response pattern and remained generally consistent across multiple sensitivity analyses. Exploratory mediation analysis suggested that white blood cell count partially mediated the observed relationships. TyG-WC is associated with increased mortality risk among individuals with overweight or obesity and may represent a complementary marker for risk assessment, pending further prospective validation.

title: Post-weaning audiovisual overstimulation induces autism-like phenotypes and amygdala structural plasticity in rats.
abstract: The rapid rise in childhood exposure to digital devices has raised concerns about its impact on brain development and its potential link to autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Recent studies have shown that when excessive exposure to digital devices begins during early development (before weaning), it can lead to behavioral disturbances, including hyperactivity and social deficits along with impaired brain neuroplasticity in animal models. This study aimed to investigate whether prolonged excessive audiovisual stimulation (EAVS) after weaning could induce autism-like symptoms in rats. While this model does not fully capture the voluntary nature of human device use, it provides a controlled experimental framework for examining the neurobiological consequences of sensory overstimulation during development. Male rats were exposed to colored lights and cartoon sounds for 6 h daily from postnatal day (PND) 22 to PND 52. Behavioral assessments and 3-D stereological measurement were conducted to evaluate autism-related behaviors and amygdala structure in adolescence. The results revealed increased repetitive behaviors, impaired social interaction, hyperactivity, and significant enlargement of the amygdala, along with an increased number of neurons in its basolateral (BL) and central (CE) subregions. This study suggests that the negative effects of overexposure to digital devices are not limited to infancy. Prolonged exposure to EAVS during childhood can lead to changes in amygdala structure and the emergence of behavioral impairments similar to ASD.

title: Combined Pyruvate, Coenzyme Q10, and Nicotinamide Supplementation Preserves Mitochondrial Function and Axonal Integrity in Retinal Ganglion Cells.
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction and NAD+ depletion are increasingly recognized as central contributors to neurodegeneration, including glaucoma. Retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) are particularly susceptible to metabolic stress due to their high energetic demand, suggesting that strategies aimed at restoring mitochondrial bioenergetics may provide neuroprotection. Here, we evaluated combined supplementation with pyruvate (Pyr), coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10), and nicotinamide (B3) to simultaneously support mitochondrial substrate availability, oxidative phosphorylation, and NAD+ homeostasis. Using human astrocytoma cells under metabolic stress, combined treatment restored cell growth, increased ATP and NAD(H) levels, reduced oxidative stress and inflammation, and preserved mitochondrial membrane potential and network morphology. The neuroprotective efficacy of the combined treatment was validated in primary murine RGCs using microfluidic axotomy models. Treatment significantly reduced axonal degeneration and promoted regeneration after injury. Live-cell ATP imaging demonstrated that the treatment preserved intra-axonal ATP levels after axotomy, indicating improved energy resilience during injury-induced stress. These findings suggest that coordinated metabolic support enhances mitochondrial function and resilience in RGCs, highlighting a promising approach to neuroprotection in glaucoma by targeting mitochondrial metabolism and redox balance.

title: Cilostazol for Secondary Prevention of Stroke and Cognitive Decline: An Updated Systematic Review.
journal: International journal of stroke : official journal of the International Stroke Society
abstract: Cilostazol may benefit secondary stroke prevention and cerebral small vessel disease (SVD). Evidence for its role in preventing recurrent stroke and cognitive decline, particularly after lacunar stroke, remains limited although evolving. We updated a previous systematic review to evaluate cilostazol effects on long-term outcomes after stroke or cognitive decline. The protocol was registered on PROSPERO and conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. We searched MEDLINE and EMBASE from January 2019 to August 2026 for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of cilostazol, alone or with other antiplatelets, in adults with stroke, SVD, or cognitive impairment. We cross-checked prior searches (1990 - 2019) and manually checked additional relevant sources. Meta-analyses and sensitivity analyses were performed where possible with data from the previous review. Twenty-one publications were identified since 2019, including 14 new RCTs, which synthesised with 20 previous trials, gave 34 RCTs overall (n=16,740). Cilostazol reduced recurrent ischemic stroke (OR 0.75 [95% CI 0.65-0.87]), hemorrhagic stroke (OR 0.46 [0.33-0.66]), all stroke (OR 0.68 [0.59-0.77]), major cardiovascular event (OR 0.71 [0.61-0.82]), dependency (OR 0.86 [0.73-0.99]) and depression (OR 0.33 [0.20-0.53]), with a non-significant trend towards improved mood scores. The reduction in ischemic stroke was most consistently observed in chronic-phase long-term trials and those with ≥40% lacunar stroke, although the associations in meta-regression were weak and further attenuated after adjustment for comparator antiplatelet regimens. Trials reporting cognitive function were sparse and methodologically inconsistent, without clear effects on cognitive scores. Cilostazol increased headache, palpitations, diarrhoea, dizziness, and tachycardia or arrhythmia. Cilostazol appears effective and safe for long-term secondary stroke prevention, including after lacunar stroke, while its effects on cognition and mood require confirmation in further randomised trials.

title: Gaps and Recommendations for Universal Eating Disorder Screening in Youth: Proposal of a Novel Screening Tool.
journal: The International journal of eating disorders
abstract: Eating disorders (EDs) are common in youth, yet often under-detected in pediatric healthcare settings due to lack of universal screening. This is a significant gap in the ED field. Current ED screening tools are not well-validated in youth, were not designed to detect symptoms across sociodemographic groups, anthropometric classes, and symptom presentations, and do not include parent/caregiver input. Our group has worked with key stakeholders to develop a novel ED screening tool for youth that was designed for use in the primary care and specialty settings, the Screening Kids And Teens for Eating disorders (SKATE), child (C-SKATE) and parent/caregiver (P-SKATE) versions. One hundred forty six 8-18-year-olds and their parent/caregiver at two sites completed the C-SKATE and P-SKATE, respectively. Children completed the diagnostic section of the Eating Disorder Examination (EDE) or the full EDE. A subset of youth repeated the C-SKATE 2 weeks later. Internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha) for the C-SKATE and P-SKATE were 0.75 (95% CI: 0.68, 0.81) and 0.76 (0.69, 0.81), respectively. Test-retest reliability was strong, with an intraclass correlation for total C-SKATE score of 0.89 (95% CI: 0.74-0.95, p < 0.001). Overall agreement and specificity were high for behaviors when comparing SKATE items to diagnostic items on the EDE. Among those completing the full EDE, the SKATE showed moderately strong positive correlations with the EDE Shape- and Weight-Concern subscales. Next research steps include validation in larger, more representative clinical and community samples, consideration of potential harms of screening, studying implementation factors, and examining the SKATE in high-risk and under-represented groups.

title: Not the chosen one: Aftereffects of nonselected responses.
abstract: In choice reaction tasks, correctly chosen responses have aftereffects on subsequent responding (e.g., response repetition benefits), and so have incorrectly chosen responses (e.g., posterror slowing). Here we studied whether correct but not chosen responses exert similar aftereffects. Doing so allows us to assess whether codes of possible but eventually not executed action alternatives become inhibited, because they lost response competition, or remain in a heightened activation state. In three experiments, we had participants in a prime trial freely choose among two response alternatives, while a third response alternative was labeled as invalid. In a subsequent probe trial, we measured the performance of these three responses in a forced-choice reaction task. In the probe trial, we observed benefits for the feasible but not chosen prime response compared with the execution of a previously invalid response. The results suggest a sustained activation of unexecuted action alternatives. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Aftereffects of response selection have primarily been investigated in forced-choice scenarios, in which nonselected correct responses can be examined only following errors. In this article, we show that aftereffects also occur for nonselected, yet feasible, responses in free-choice scenarios. These effects became smaller as free choices grew more biased, suggesting that they depend on the extent to which the nonselected response functioned as a genuine competitor. Our results suggest that nonselected responses continue to influence later behavior when they function as genuine alternatives during action selection. OPEN PRACTICES STATEMENT: The trial-level data and analysis code for all experiments are publicly available on OSF ( https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/V524H ). Experiment 1 b was preregistered ( https://aspredicted.org/9bq4zg.pdf ).

title: Methionine restriction and its underlying molecular mechanisms in brain health and diseases.
abstract: Sulfur-containing amino acids, particularly methionine, play a central role in brain metabolism and the maintenance of neural homeostasis. Perturbations in brain methionine metabolism have been associated with a wide spectrum of behavioral and neuropsychiatric outcomes, including anxiety- and depression-like phenotypes, as well as cognitive and behavioral impairments relevant to schizophrenia, fear processing, and bipolar disorder. In addition, brain methionine metabolism intersects with multiple molecular pathways implicated in major neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis, and Parkinson's disease. Accumulating evidence over the past two decades indicates that methionine intake and the integrity of the methionine metabolic network constitute a critical regulatory axis in brain health, capable of exerting both neuroprotective and neurotoxic effects in a context-dependent manner. Moderate dietary methionine restriction induces adaptive metabolic reprogramming in the brain, enhancing learning, memory, adult neurogenesis, and synaptic resilience, while simultaneously strengthening antioxidant defenses and resistance to oxidative stress. In contrast, excessive methionine intake disrupts neuronal homeostasis, promotes microglial activation, and amplifies neuroinflammatory signaling, thereby compromising neural integrity. Notably, these effects exhibit pronounced sex specificity, highlighting the modulatory roles of hormonal and genetic factors in methionine metabolism. Elucidating this duality may enable the development of precision-based dietary and metabolic interventions targeting methionine-related pathways for the prevention and treatment of psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. This review summarizes current research on dietary methionine restriction and its effects on neurological function, psychiatric conditions, and neurodegenerative diseases, with a particular focus on the underlying molecular mechanisms.

title: Primary hypogonadism in ADPRS (ADPRHL2)-related neurodegeneration: expanding the phenotypic spectrum.
Resolvin D3 modulates disease-associated platelet phenotypes in cystic fibrosis.
abstract: Platelets (PLTs) are increasingly recognized as key regulators of inflammation and immunity, yet how they contribute to chronic diseases is still poorly understood. Cystic fibrosis (CF) is characterized by persistent neutrophilic inflammation and dysregulated resolution responses, but the mechanisms underlying CF-associated PLT dysfunction remain incompletely defined. Here, we combined proteomics, phosphoproteomics, lipidomics, and high-dimensional immunophenotyping to characterize CF-associated PLT programs. Multi-omics analyses revealed coordinated alterations in receptor expression, intracellular signaling pathways, and bioactive lipid mediator responses following stimulation in CF PLTs. Screening of specialized pro-resolving mediators identified Resolvin D3 (RvD3) as a selective modulator of CF PLT responses. Specifically, RvD3 attenuated thromboxane A2 (TxA2) biosynthesis and was associated with remodeling of signaling networks linked to PLT activation, adhesion, and PLT-leukocyte interactions. At the cellular level, high-dimensional immunophenotyping further showed that RvD3 reshaped CD41-defined PLT subpopulations characterized by distinct surface-marker profiles, indicating selective modulation of PLT phenotypic heterogeneity. In preclinical models of CF pneumonia, RvD3 reduced PLT-neutrophil interactions, improved bacterial clearance, and limited neutrophilic inflammation, while PLT depletion attenuated these effects. Together, these findings identify CF-associated PLT inflammatory programs and marker-defined PLT phenotypes, and support a model in which RvD3 modulates PLT responses linked to inflammation resolution and host defense in CF.

title: The ACOD1-itaconate axis in alzheimer's disease: immunometabolic mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by progressive cognitive decline associated with the interplay between amyloid-β (Aβ) and tau pathology, chronic neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and metabolic reprogramming of glial cells. Increasing evidence identifies immunometabolic dysregulation as a key contributor to AD pathogenesis, highlighting the aconitate decarboxylase 1 (ACOD1)/itaconate pathway as a promising therapeutic target. Itaconate, an endogenous metabolite generated from cis-aconitate by ACOD1 during immune activation, regulates inflammatory and metabolic signaling through several mechanisms, including succinate dehydrogenase inhibition, activation of the KEAP1-Nrf2 antioxidant pathway, suppression of nuclear factor-κB signaling, and modulation ofNLRP3 inflammasome activation. Through these mechanisms, itaconate may attenuate oxidative stress, modulate mitochondrial function, regulate microglial and astrocytic activation, and promote neuroimmune homeostasis. Emerging preclinical evidence further suggests that itaconate and its derivatives may attenuate Aβ-associated neuroinflammation, modulate tau-related pathological processes, preserve synaptic proteins, including synaptophysin and postsynaptic density protein 95 (PSD-95), and improve cognitive performance in experimental models of AD. This review critically examinesthe biosynthesis and molecular mechanisms of ACOD1-itaconate signaling, with particular emphasis on its involvement in neuroinflammation, amyloid and tau pathology, synaptic dysfunction, and glial immunometabolic reprogramming. It also discusses advances in multi-omics approaches, the development of itaconate derivatives, and potential therapeutic combinations. Finally, key translational barriers, including blood-brain barrier penetration, pharmacokinetic properties, metabolic stability, cellular specificity, and the need for clinical validation, are highlighted to define future directions for translating ACOD1-itaconate-based therapies into potential disease-modifying strategies for AD.

title: ACC Sulcal Morphology as a Neurodevelopmental Marker of Proactive and Reactive Cognitive Control among Adolescents.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Behavioral inhibition (BI) is an early temperament associated with higher risk for later anxiety. BI has been linked to variation in cognitive control, particularly proactive control, a crucial component of executive functions which involves monitoring one's own behavior and adapting that behavior to achieve a particular goal, which may help explain BI's association with elevated anxiety risk. Yet little is known about the neurobiology of cognitive control development among children with BI. Variation in anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) sulcal pattern asymmetry, established prenatally and stable across development, is associated with individual differences in cognitive control. This preliminary study examined whether ACC sulcal symmetry is associated with BI, proactive and reactive control (measured via the AX-CPT) in adolescents. Structural T1-weighted MRI was acquired from 62 adolescents aged 12 to 15 years. ACC patterns in each hemisphere were classified as 'single type' or 'double parallel type' based on the presence of a paracingulate sulcus. Adolescents with symmetric ACC patterns showed lower proactive control ( d' context; η²p = .091) and greater reactive control (BX probe interference effect; η²p = .119). These associations held even when tested within the same statistical model and were comparable in magnitude. ACC symmetry was not associated with BI, nor did it interact with BI to predict cognitive control scores. Overall, the findings provide preliminary evidence that ACC sulcal morphology may be a structural marker of variability in cognitive control, with relevance to BI-related neurocognitive risk.

title: The ANKLE2-VRK1 pathway promotes neuronal resilience by preserving proteostasis during aging.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: ANKLE2 is a key regulator of neural stem cell division through inhibition of the kinase VRK1, and mutations in either ANKLE2 or VRK1 cause rare neurodevelopmental disorders that impact brain growth and development. Recent evidence showing that reduced ANKLE2 activity promotes Tau aggregation in vitro suggests that ANKLE2 may also contribute to age-related neurodegenerative processes; however, its role post-development remains unknown. Using Drosophila , we show a novel role for the Ankle2 - ballchen ( VRK1 ) pathway in maintaining neuronal resilience and proteostasis. Pan-neuronal and motor neuron reduction of Ankle2 in adult animals shortens lifespan, impairs motor function and accelerates neuronal loss. Lifelong reduction produces more severe phenotypes including an upright wing posture reminiscent of Drosophila Parkinson's disease models. Mechanistically, loss of Ankle2 causes the accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins throughout the central nervous system, indicating impaired protein clearance. Ankle2 mutants have reduced proteasome activity with activation of compensatory degradative pathways, supporting this hypothesis. Loss of Ankle2 behavioral and protein accumulation phenotypes are rescued by expression of human ANKLE2, indicating neuronal ANKLE2 function is conserved between flies and humans. Importantly, VRK1/Ballchen reduction also rescues ubiquitin accumulation and behavior phenotypes caused by loss of Ankle2 , demonstrating that the developmental Ankle2-VRK1 pathway is preserved and remains functionally important in aged neurons. More broadly, our findings reveal that a conserved developmental ANKLE2-VRK1 pathway is repurposed in aged neurons to maintain proteostasis and neuronal resilience, providing a mechanistic framework linking neurodevelopmental disease genes to age-associated neurodegeneration.

title: Doublecortin like kinase 1 (DCLK1) interacts with BRG1 chromatin remodeler and regulates neuronal activity-induced gene activation.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: SWI/SNF-like BAF ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complexes play important roles in neural development and plasticity by regulating neural gene expression, especially in response to neuronal stimulations. Previously, we have shown that BRG1, the core subunit of BAF, undergoes neuronal activity-induced phosphorylation, which is important for the expression of a group of activity regulated genes (ARGs). Proteomic analyses identified Doublecortin like kinase 1 (DCLK1) as a novel BRG1 interacting protein. Neuronal depolarization induces nuclear enrichment of DCLK1 and increases interactions between BRG1 and DCLK1. We showed that the DCLK1 kinase domain and BRG1 C-terminal fragments are sufficient to mediate their interaction. Thus, DCLK1 is a candidate kinase responsible for BRG1 phosphorylation in response to neuronal activation. Using DCLK1 specific inhibitors and kinase inactive mutations, we showed that DCLK1, in a kinase activity dependent manner, promotes BRG1 phosphorylation and ARG activation. Thus, we identified a novel interacting kinase of BAF chromatin remodeling complex that regulates ARG expression. Because abnormal expression and mutations of both BAF complexes and DCLK1 are associated with neural disorders and cancer, our study provides molecular insights into their functions in these diseases.

title: Programmed ribosomal frameshifting regulates tissue-specific pioneer activity.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Pioneer transcription factors bind nucleosomal DNA and establish accessible chromatin, yet their binding is tissue specific 1-5 . While studies have largely focused on protein-extrinsic features, like chromatin structure and cofactor expression, the mechanisms governing the tissue-specific binding remain poorly understood. We used the Drosophila pioneer transcription factor Zelda as a paradigm to investigate the mechanisms controlling tissue-specific binding. Zelda promotes the undifferentiated state in both the embryo and in neural stem cells of the larval brain 6-10 . However, Zelda binds thousands of unique sites in each tissue and, in so doing, defines tissue-specific enhancers 6 . We showed that tissue-specific binding is controlled by the developmentally regulated use of two distinct DNA-binding domains. Our identification of a novel, neural stem cell enriched Zelda proteoform that lacks the embryo-specific C-terminal DNA-binding domain explains the differential DNA-binding domain usage. This proteoform arises through developmentally regulated -1 ribosomal frameshifting, a mechanism common to viruses but not documented for any eukaryotic transcription factors. Together we revealed a new strategy where developmentally programmed ribosomal frameshifting confers tissue-specific pioneer-factor binding and suggest that this mechanism may be more broadly used to diversify the proteome than previously appreciated.

title: Endothelial VCAM1 links oncogenic KRAS signaling to myeloid inflammation and hemorrhagic instability in brain arteriovenous malformations.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Hemorrhagic conversion is the most devastating complication of brain arteriovenous malformations (bAVMs). However, endothelial mechanisms promoting macrophages (Mϕ) recruitment, microglia (MG) activation, and bAVM lesion instability remain unclear. We investigated vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM1) as a mediator linking oncogenic endothelial signaling to myeloid cell responses and hemorrhagic progression in bAVMs. We performed integrated transcriptomic analysis of human bAVM and epilepsy-control brain tissues, with validation in local bAVM specimens. Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses of bAVM lesions and intact brain tissues from mutant KRAS-induced bAVM mice were followed by histological validation. Using AAV-BR1-KRAS G12V -injected Cx3cr1-gfp;Ccr2-rfp mice, we performed intravital imaging to assess Mϕ/MG responses to VCAM1 neutralization. Hemorrhage and myeloid cell responses were also evaluated following endothelial-specific VCAM1 deletion . Plasma soluble VCAM1 (sVCAM1) was measured in patients with unruptured and ruptured bAVMs and unruptured aneurysm controls. Effects of sVCAM1 on MG activation were examined in vitro . Integrated human endothelial bulk and single-cell RNA-sequencing and tissue validation identified VCAM1 upregulation in bAVMs, including unruptured lesions. Plasma analyses showed increased sVCAM1 in unruptured and ruptured bAVM patients compared with unruptured aneurysm controls. In mutant KRAS-induced bAVM mice, transcriptomic and proteomic analyses demonstrated increased VCAM1 expression, with endothelial localization confirmed histologically. In vitro, mutant KRAS increased sVCAM1 production, while recombinant sVCAM1 stimulated inflammatory mediator expression in MG. Both MG and Mϕ expressed VLA-4, a major VCAM1 receptor. Intravital imaging showed that VCAM1 neutralization reduced Mϕ accumulation and MG activation, while early VCAM1 neutralization reduced hemorrhagic burden. Consistently, endothelial-specific VCAM1 deletion reduced Mϕ accumulation, MG activation, and hemorrhage volume in bAVM mice and improved behavioral performance. These findings identify endothelial VCAM1 as an upstream mediator linking mutant KRAS signaling to myeloid cell responses and hemorrhagic progression in bAVMs. This study establishes endothelial VCAM1 as a potential therapeutic target for attenuating hemorrhagic progression. What is Known?: Brain arteriovenous malformations (bAVMs) are a major cause of hemorrhagic stroke and neurological disability or death. Somatic activating KRAS mutations in endothelial cells drive abnormal angiogenic signaling and are detected in more than 72% of sporadic bAVMs.Microglia/macrophages (MG/Mϕ) accumulate in unruptured human and mouse bAVMs. Our previous studies demonstrated that MG/Mϕ-mediated vascular inflammation contributes to blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, bAVM instability, and hemorrhagic conversion in mouse bAVMs.VCAM1-VLA-4 signaling is an established mechanism of myeloid cell adhesion and recruitment, including macrophage recruitment, however, whether endothelial VCAM1 contributes to inflammatory bAVM instability and hemorrhagic conversion in bAVMs remains unknown.What new information does this article contribute?: Endothelial VCAM1 is identified as an upstream mediator linking oncogenic KRAS signaling to inflammatory MG/Mϕ responses in bAVMs. Integrated human and mouse transcriptomic and proteomic analyses, together with histological validation, identify endothelial VCAM1 as a conserved and markedly upregulated molecular feature of bAVMs. Endothelial-derived soluble VCAM1 (sVCAM1) provides a potential mechanism for endothelial-microglial communication. Plasma sVCAM1 levels were elevated in patients with unruptured bAVMs compared with unruptured aneurysm controls, with a trend toward further elevation in ruptured bAVMs. Mutant KRAS increased endothelial sVCAM1 production, and sVCAM1 stimulated microglial activation in vitro , identifying a potential mechanism by which mutant endothelial cells promote brain-resident immune cell activation. Endothelial VCAM1 contributes functionally to myeloid cell responses and hemorrhagic instability in bAVMs. Pharmacological VCAM1 neutralization reduced Mϕ infiltration, MG activation, and early bleeding in mouse bAVMs, whereas endothelial-specific VCAM1 deletion reduced Mϕ infiltration, MG activation, and hemorrhage volume. These complementary loss-of-function approaches establish endothelial VCAM1 as a functional mediator of inflammatory bAVM instability. Hemorrhagic conversion is the most devastating complication of bAVMs, yet the endothelial mechanisms that initiate inflammatory responses and promote bAVM lesion instability remain poorly understood. Because early Mϕ infiltration and MG activation contribute to BBB disruption and hemorrhagic conversion, identifying the upstream endothelial signals that drive these responses may reveal new approaches to stabilize bAVMs. Through cross-validation of independent human transcriptomics datasets and orthogonal analyses of human bAVM tissues, we identified endothelial VCAM1 as a consistently elevated molecular feature of bAVMs. Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic analyses, in vivo imaging, pharmacological neutralization, and endothelial-specific genetic loss-of-function studies further demonstrate that VCAM1 links oncogenic KRAS signaling to Mϕ recruitment, MG activation, and hemorrhagic instability. In addition, our findings identify endothelial-derived sVCAM1 as a potential paracrine signal capable of activating MG. Together, these findings establish endothelial VCAM1 as a functional mediator of the inflammatory axis connecting oncogenic vascular signaling to myeloid cell responses and hemorrhagic instability in bAVMs. This study identifies VCAM1 as a potential therapeutic target for limiting hemorrhagic progression and provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how oncogenic endothelial signaling contributes to inflammatory vascular dysfunction beyond bAVMs.

title: Rare miRNA variants in complex neuropsychiatric pedigrees alter synaptic miRNA gene-targets.
journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
abstract: Although rare non-coding variants are likely involved in psychiatric disorder susceptibility, their contribution is poorly understood. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) regulate gene expression, and targets in the brain include genes involved in neuronal development and synaptic plasticity. Because single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) can alter miRNA processing and target specificity, this can have disproportionate downstream impact on multiple genes affecting pathways that regulate biological processes, making them compelling candidates for mediating psychiatric disorder risk. We investigated rare miRNA variants in whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from 25 pedigrees with diagnoses including schizophrenia, psychosis, bipolar disorder, depression, OCD, and substance use disorder. Evidence of segregation with schizophrenia and related psychotic disorders was identified for five rare miRNA variants (two seed-region, one mature-region, and two precursor-region variants), including a SNV in the mature-region of miR-4794, segregating strongly in two unrelated pedigrees and identified in a parent-offspring pair with schizophrenia from a third pedigree. One of these two pedigrees also segregates a seed-region SNV in miR-4423-3p, predicted to significantly impact expression-regulation, causing the loss of synaptic gene-targets associated with psychiatric disorders. Collectively, targets of three of the miRNAs are enriched for schizophrenia rare variant risk genes (p-value: 0.00027): six SCHEMA genes were targeted by miR-96 and four genes by miR-4423-3p. While further understanding of miRNA function and validation is required, this study demonstrates the value of integrating structural modelling, target-shift prediction, and pathway enrichment to interpret non-coding variants. This highlights the utility of WGS for identifying and investigating rare non-coding variation in psychiatric disorder susceptibility, supplementing exome-based approaches.

title: Plasma neurodegeneration biomarkers and clinical progression in early sporadic Parkinson's disease.
journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
abstract: Plasma neurodegeneration biomarkers offer an opportunity to characterize Parkinson's disease (PD) biology. The objective of this study was to investigate such biomarkers in deeply-phenotyped participants in Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI). Baseline plasma samples from early (<2 years since diagnosis) sporadic PD participants with a positive CSF alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay (aSyn-SAA) and healthy controls (HC) with a negative aSyn-SAA test were utilized. Plasma P-tau217 (Roche Diagnostics), neurofilament light chain (NfL, Quanterix), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP, Quanterix), and (PD only) amyloid-beta (Aβ) levels (40 and 42, C2N Diagnostics) were measured. Clinical features at baseline and over up to 11 years were compared across biomarker tertiles in models controlling for age, sex, and baseline outcome variable. The cohort was 97 HC and 523 PD and participants. Median [IQR] biomarker values (pg/mL) for HC and PD were P-tau217: 0.14 [0.06 -0.75], 0.15 [0.06 -0.90]; NfL: 10.6 [3.13 - 49.85], 12.26 [3.77-62.67]; GFAP: 66.56 [19.75 -403.48], 87.19 [14.55 -531.82]; and in PD Aβ40: 391.32 [209.95 -538.38]; Aβ42: 42.74[27.75 -68.55]. No biomarkers differed between HC and PD. In PD, biomarkers were associated with age. In PD only, higher baseline levels of P-tau217 and NfL were associated with greater hazards of a worse cognitive and balance outcome. P-tau217, NfL, and GFAP levels were associated with change in cognitive score over time. Plasma P-tau217, NfL and GFAP levels in early, sporadic PD with confirmed synucleinopathy predict future cognitive and functional impairment, and these findings can inform clinical research design and clinical care.

title: Cortical surface area is an independent predictor of incident dementia.
journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
abstract: Cortical surface area (cSA) is associated with intelligence and cognition, yet structural MRI studies of neurodegeneration in Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) have emphasized quantification of cortical thickness (cTH) and volume, with very limited evaluation of cSA. We examined whether cSA of AD-relevant brain regions provide diagnostic, prognostic, and biological information beyond cTH and volume across 5,430 participants (3,124 cognitively unimpaired; 1,634 mild cognitive impairment [MCI]; 672 ADRD) from three aging and dementia cohorts: the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center, Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, and Carotids and Minds study. In cross-sectional analyses, cSA and cTH showed weak correlation, and lower cSA was independently associated with greater odds of MCI and ADRD after adjustment for cTH and covariates. Participants with both low cSA and low cTH had greater risk of MCI and ADRD compared to low cSA, cTH, or volume alone. In longitudinal models, baseline cSA predicted incident ADRD independent from cTH, and combined cSA/cTH models outperformed cSA, cTH, or volume alone for predicting incident ADRD over a mean follow-up of 4.3 years. Complementing these findings, proteomics analyses revealed distinct signatures associated with cSA compared to cTH. Overall, these findings support cSA as a clinically informative and biologically distinct dimension of AD-related cortical vulnerability.

title: The social conditioned place preference assay is sensitive to drug dose, training regimen, and social context.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Beginning in the 1960s, researchers have understood that one of the unique properties of psychedelic drugs is that their effects are modified by the context in which they are taken (also known as their 'set' and 'setting' dependence). To date, 7 different studies have shown that critical period reopening is a shared property across psychedelic drugs, including ketamine, MDMA, psilocybin, LSD, and ibogaine. Moreover, the context dependence of psychedelics' effects has been recapitulated for both MDMA and ketamine. Recently, Lu et al., Nature Neuroscience 2026 (PMID: 42972049) have claimed that psilocybin does not reopen the social reward learning critical period, which the authors interpret as a failure to replicate previously published results. Here, we re-analyzed results across three published datasets (Nardou et al., Nature 2019; Nardou et al., Nature 2023; Lu et al., Nature Neuroscience 2026) in order to compare the impact of dose, training regimen, and social context on the social conditioned place preference (social CPP) assay. Our analysis reveals that methodological modifications likely account for Lu and colleagues' inability to reopen the social reward learning critical period with psilocybin. Nevertheless, because their results recapitulate previous findings that psychedelics' effects are context dependent, they support rather than challenge the growing literature demonstrating that psychedelics reopen critical periods.

title: Parvalbumin interneuron circuit sharpens orientation tuning via the extraclassical surround in cat V1.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Parvalbumin-expressing (PV) inhibitory neurons are central to cortical gain control, yet optogenetic studies disagree on whether they sharpen orientation tuning or merely rescale responses. Because this work has been performed almost exclusively in rodents, which lack orientation columns and an orientation-matched extraclassical surround, the contribution of surround circuitry has remained untested. Here we combine cell-type-specific rabies-virus tracing with optogenetics to activate or suppress PV circuits in cat primary visual cortex, and measure single-neuron orientation tuning for stimuli confined to the classical receptive field or extending into the extraclassical surround. Activating PV circuits sharpened tuning progressively with illumination power for classical-receptive-field stimuli, but left tuning unchanged once the surround was engaged; conversely, suppressing them broadened tuning only for surround-engaging stimuli and left classical-receptive-field tuning unchanged. This double dissociation places PV circuitry in the causal path that sets tuning width and identifies surround suppression as the inhibition it supplies: where the surround is not recruited there is little PV-mediated inhibition to remove, and where it is, removing that inhibition widens tuning. PV-dependent sharpening is therefore bounded by the receptive-field architecture through which the population is recruited, not by a fixed property of the PV population itself.

title: Distinct Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging-Derived White Matter Microstructural Phenotypes Tracking Alzheimer's Disease Pathology and Cognitive Decline.
journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
abstract: White matter (WM) pathology is increasingly recognized as an early, mechanistically relevant feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet sensitive in-vivo biomarkers remain limited. Here, we introduce an MRI-based Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging (RKI) technique sensitive to WM microstructure. RKI metrics differentiate two distinct phenotypes of white matter that follow divergent microstructural trajectories in preclinical and early symptomatic AD. We examined their relationships to AD progression, gray matter (GM) pathology, and clinical impairment in 305 adults spanning amyloid-negative to amyloid-positive stages with normal cognition, preclinical AD, and early symptomatic AD. Pathological changes in one phenotype reflected axonal alterations without myelin loss and were anatomically coupled to GM cortical pathology, strengthening with disease stage - a signature of Wallerian degeneration. Alterations in the other phenotype represented WM demyelination. A model incorporating RKI-metrics, age, sex, amyloid status, APOE genotype, and brain volume classified Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR)-based impairment with an area under the receiver operating curve (AUC) = 0.933, with the RKI-metrics contributing 27% (second only to amyloid at 40%). While both phenotypes related comparably to concurrent cognition (each ∼27%), the "axonal" phenotype showed the strongest relationship to subsequent cognitive decline (41% of explained variance), with the "myelin" phenotype contributing 31%. These RKI-defined dual white matter phenotypes provide new insight into AD pathology, adding diagnostic and prognostic value for tracking both current cognitive status and future cognitive decline. A new MRI-based Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging (RKI) method characterizes two distinct white matter tissue signatures that track Alzheimer's progression, predicting both clinical dementia stage and future cognitive decline. Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging (RKI) differentiates two distinct microstructural phenotypes with different trajectories of white matter pathology in Alzheimer's disease.The first phenotype highlights microstructural axonal alterations anatomically coupled to regional cortical pathology consistent with Wallerian neurodegeneration.The second phenotype represents demyelination diffusely connected to cortical pathology.RKI metrics track AD pathology and predict future cognitive decline.

title: Data-Driven Decomposition of Precisely Aligned Fiber-Orientation-Preserving Probabilistic Tractography Connectomes with Non-Negative Matrix Factorization.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: The major goals of the Human Connectome Project (HCP) were to characterize the structural and functional connectivity of the human brain. Although there has been tremendous work done for functional connectivity, including application of a variety of data driven decomposition approaches, structural connectivity from the HCP has seen less attention. This work presents a collection of methodological advances that, in combination, enable similar approaches to be applied to diffusion tractography data. Here, we use multi-modal non-linear volumetric alignment with FSL's MultiMOdal Registration Framework (MMORF) to precisely align white matter tracts and globular gray matter nuclei, use the White matter Hierarchical Modelling (WHIM) method to align voxel-wise fiber orientations, enable efficient GPU-accelerated computation and storage of full resolution probabilistic gray matter x white matter x fiber sparse tractography matrices in precise alignment across individuals using the aforementioned MMORF and WHIM alignments together with areal-feature-based cortical surface registration. These tractography dense connectomes can be averaged across individuals and sparse, computationally efficient non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) can be applied to perform data-driven decompositions into white matter tracts and gray matter projection territories. The primary outputs of this effort to date are 1) A set of HCP software pipelines enabling such analyses, 2) A new unbiased HCP-derived volumetric standard space that is representative of the young adult brain and follows ACPC orientation conventions across individuals. 3) Reproducible NMF decompositions of HCP young adult tractography data into white matter tracts and gray matter projection territories, which could be projected using non-negative dual regression back to individuals. These data represent a starting point for a new generation of data-driven atlasing efforts for human white matter, and these methods can be applied to study the white matter in development, aging, and brain diseases.

title: Diffusion-based vertex-wise connectomics encodes individual differences in cognition, affect and pathology.
journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
abstract: No two brains are wired alike, and much of a person's cognitive and clinical state is written in this individual variation, not in the group average. Structural connectomes, however, are typically read through group atlases that summarize connectivity into regional averages, leaving this individual signal untapped. We build a vertex-wise structural connectome, in which every cortical surface vertex is a node, and apply it across the Alzheimer's continuum. Using an independent dataset for methodological development and a multisite cohort of 317 participants from ADNI-4, we show that connection distance and organizational scale form a nested hierarchy, from a long-range backbone to fine, short-range structure. The individual fingerprint is strongest in medium- and short-range connections and becomes less distinctive as connectivity is pooled into atlas parcels. This individual structure can be recovered across spatial scales, although its fidelity depends on diffusion acquisition quality, with multishell data providing a more informative reference than single-shell data. In the aging brain, an individually referenced balance between short- and long-range connectivity is associated with episodic memory, cognitive reserve, depressive symptoms, and shared molecular pathology. While cognitive associations largely reflect diagnostic differences, associations with depressive symptoms and pathology burden remain detectable after adjustment for diagnosis. These findings show that individual structural connectomes retain clinically and biologically relevant variation that is not fully captured by diagnostic classification or group-level summaries.

title: Nose-to-Brain Delivery of Cocaine in Mice: A Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic Model Incorporating Olfactory Epithelial Transport, Mucociliary Clearance, and Blood-Brain Barrier Permeability.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Intranasal (IN) cocaine produces rapid central nervous system (CNS) effects despite generating substantially lower plasma concentrations than equivalent intravenous (IV) doses, suggesting a direct nose-to-brain pathway. The olfactory epithelium provides anatomical continuity for cocaine to pass between the nasal cavity and the brain. Quantifying the relative contribution of this pathway to total brain cocaine exposure requires a physiologically-based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model that explicitly accounts for nasal mucosal architecture, epithelial transport barriers, and blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability. Here we used tandem mass spectrometry to collect cocaine concentration-time data from the brain and plasma of awake mice administered IV or IN cocaine and leveraged that data to generate such a framework. Our results provide evidence that following IN cocaine, the olfactory pathway accounts for approximately half of the cocaine that reaches the brain. The mechanistic PBPK framework developed here - incorporating anatomically grounded nasal compartment separation, blood-flow-scaled mucosal absorption, tissue diffusion resistance, mucociliary clearance, plasma protein binding, and BBB permeability-surface area transport - substantially improves upon empirical one-compartment absorption models and produces parameter estimates with physiological interpretability. The proportionate efficiency of the olfactory route relative to systemic absorption may provide a pharmacokinetic basis for the rapid onset of IN cocaine's CNS effects and has direct implications for understanding the psychoactive effects of cocaine. Many drugs of abuse are inhaled, including cocaine, yet the mechanistic outcomes of inhaled cocaine are not understood compared to actions of cocaine following other ROAs. We established the pharmacokinetics of IN cocaine in awake mice, and developed a PBPK model to define the contributions of the olfactory pathway upon IN cocaine administration. Our findings demonstrate the contributions of a direct nose-to-brain pathway in mediating cocaine brain entry, thus, establishing the nasal ROA as a biological variable shaping pharmacokinetics and neurobiological outcomes of cocaine.

title: LUHMES neurospheres as a novel model for the study of human neurotoxoplasmosis.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Toxoplasma gondii is a protozoan parasite that infects animal hosts for life due to its ability to persist as latent cysts inside tissues and organs, including the brain. Current treatments fail to target tissue cysts, which can recrudesce into life-threatening acute infection, and the presence of chronic infection in the brain has been linked to neurological and behavioral anomalies. The effects of the parasite on human neurons remain poorly understood, in part because reliable experimental models are limited. Here, we describe a LUnd Human Mesencephalic (LUHMES) neurosphere model to study neuronal T. gondii infection for up to 21 days. We leveraged this model to compare T. gondii infection in developing and mature neurons and observed spontaneous differentiation of tachyzoites into bradyzoite tissue cysts within neurospheres. We further show that maturation and cell-cycle state of the neuronal population influence the developmental fate of T. gondii . Transcriptomic analysis revealed that responses to infection vary with neuronal developmental state, with infection-associated changes in pathways related to synaptic function, neurogenesis, immune and inflammatory responses, metabolism, homeostasis, and neurodegeneration. We also demonstrate the utility of LUHMES neurospheres as an anti-parasitic drug screening platform, showing that the small molecule salubrinal significantly reduces the number of tissue cysts. Given that LUHMES neurospheres are genetically manipulable and can be co-cultured with glial cells, this model provides for a new and versatile platform that enables studies of parasite persistence, neuron-pathogen interactions, and drug discovery. Toxoplasma gondii causes an incurable parasitic infection that remains in the brain for life. Studying how the parasite affects human neurons may help explain how it persists and contributes to neurological changes. We adapted a laboratory "neurosphere" model using LUHMES cells, which progress from developing to mature human dopaminergic neurons. Mirroring human brain infection, the parasite transitions into the cyst stage associated with long-term, chronic infection in the LUHMES neurospheres. By comparing changes in gene expression, we found that neuronal responses to T. gondii infection differ depending on their maturation state. We also show that the neurospheres can be used to screen for new drugs that target the parasite. This versatile neurosphere model provides a powerful new tool to study T. gondii infection in the brain.

title: WormIE: an Integrated Explorer for multi-source Caenorhabditis elegans annotations and transcriptomic data interpretation.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Interpreting gene lists and expression data from Caenorhabditis elegans experiments usually means writing scripts, searching scattered databases or uploading unpublished data to a remote server. WormIE (Worm Integrated Explorer, https://wormie.bio ) is a free, open-source tool for analyzing userprovided data and exploring C. elegans annotations in one browser tab. Starting with gene lists from - omics experiments, genetic screens or other approaches, users can explore what genes have in common and how they interact, test over-representation or ranked-list enrichment in built-in or user-provided gene sets and compare lists by their genes or enriched categories. Of WormIE's nine collections, which include Gene Ontology and CeNGEN neuron types, two are curated sets found in no other worm resource: neuronal genes and synaptic genes. WormIE counts aligned reads from RNA sequencing and tests for differential expression with the same R package as conventional pipelines, then checks the genes for enrichment in those collections. Clicking any gene in a result page opens the gene page gathering seventeen domains from WormBase, the Alliance of Genome Resources and other sources, such as phenotypes, interactions and expression. Everything runs on the user's computer without uploading data and works offline. On simulated data, every analysis agreed with its R counterpart (correlation ≥ 0.9999), and in a reanalysis of a germline study of the co-regulator SIN-3, WormIE recovered 99% of the reported differentially expressed genes and all nine WormCat categories. Together, these results show that WormIE reliably links gene lists and expression data to communitycurated knowledge without programming or a server.

title: State-dependent gating of sensory and cortical inputs by median raphe neurons.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: The mesopontine median raphe (MnR) plays an important role in regulating brain states, hippocampal network activity, and memory processes. Recent studies have revealed that the MnR comprises three major neuronal populations: serotonergic (5-HT), glutamatergic (Vglut3-expressing), and GABAergic neurons. How these distinct neuronal populations may gate sensory and cortical inputs across different brain states remains largely unknown. Here, we combined in vivo electrophysiological recording, sensory or optogenetic stimulation, and transgenic approaches to characterize the response properties of 5-HT, Vglut3, and GABAergic MnR neurons during wakefulness and sleep. We found that MnR neurons exhibited pronounced state-dependent responses to both sensory and cortical stimulation, with response amplitudes significantly greater during slow-wave sleep than during wakefulness. Auditory and somatosensory stimuli elicited fast responses in the MnR: 5-HT neurons were primarily suppressed, whereas Vglut3 and GABAergic neurons were primarily activated, suggesting the presence of direct inputs from sensory thalamic or brainstem structures. Retrograde tracing identified several brainstem structures and, notably, the medial prefrontal cortex as sources of direct projections to the MnR. Optogenetic stimulation of prefrontal inputs to the MnR evoked inhibition of 5-HT neurons but robust excitation of Vglut3 neurons during slow-wave sleep, suggesting top-down control of MnR activity by the prefrontal cortex. Together, these findings reveal that the MnR exhibits enhanced sensitivity to both ascending sensory and descending cortical inputs during sleep, suggesting that it may integrate environmental and cortical signals to regulate hippocampal network activity and gate sleep-dependent memory processing.

title: Preprocessing Determines Whether Fractal Biomarkers Detect Neurodegeneration: A Systematic Evaluation Across Five fMRI Pipelines.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Fractal analysis of resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) has been proposed for detecting altered neural dynamics in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but the effect of preprocessing on these measurements is poorly constrained. We evaluated 229 ADNI3 participants (156 cognitively normal [CN], 60 mild cognitive impairment [MCI], and 13 AD) processed with five ENIGMA HALFpipe variants. Each scan contained 197 volumes (TR = 3.0 s) and 434 regional time series. The reported CN-AD effect varied 4.5-fold for the detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) Hurst exponent and 13.1-fold for Sample Entropy; both measures met p < 0.05 only after aCompCor. Under aCompCor, mean H was 0.812 in CN, 0.827 in MCI, and 0.872 in AD ( d = -1.40, p = 0.0003), whereas the other four DFA effects were approximately d = -0.31 to -0.40. A variance decomposition attributed 41.5% of total H variance to pipeline, 44.5% to participant, and 0.3% to diagnosis. Whole-brain analysis found higher H in AD across 16 of 18 networks, with 36 cortical regions surviving false-discovery-rate correction. Synthetic fractional Gaussian noise experiments confirmed monotonic DFA estimation at the available scan length. The small AD group makes all disease-effect estimates exploratory. These results show that preprocessing choice can determine whether fractal group differences are detectable and should therefore be treated as part of the biomarker definition.

title: Longitudinal examination of cerebellar morphometry across typical aging adults reveals nonlinear heterogenous trends.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Cerebellar structural integrity has been associated with cognitive capability in both neurodegenerative and healthy aging populations. The understanding of regional, longitudinal cerebellar structural changes is not well studied, and with an increasing aging population, there is an increasing need to fill this gap. Moreover, traditional modeling approaches apply linear techniques, which may fail to detect possible nuanced aging patterns. The present study investigates the nonlinear effect of age on subregional cerebellar structures in healthy adults (n = 1,371), aged 36 to 90+, from the Human Connectome Project in Aging and the follow-up continuation, Aging Adult Brain Connectome studies. Subject T1w images underwent cerebellar segmentation and volumetric estimation via the Automatic Cerebellum Parcellation using U-NET with Locally Constrained Optimization (ACAPULCO) algorithm. Cross-sectional, longitudinal, and sex specific volumetric differences were examined using generalized additive mixed models. Heterogenous atrophy patterns were observed across the cerebellum; however, the majority of effects were evident in the posterior cerebellum. Longitudinal models showed nonlinear negative trends for all regions surviving correction, while baseline age effects had a combination of linear and nonlinear negative trajectories after correction. Specific sex differences emerged, where men predominantly had higher regional volumes, as well as there being sex-related influences of longitudinal morphologic patterns. Furthermore, midlife appeared as a period of structural vulnerability, demonstrating escalated volume loss. Consistent with the literature, the identified volumetric reduction patterns suggest that age effects on the cerebellum are multifaceted, with region specific alterations, highlighting the complexity of this structure.

title: Cerebellar transcranial AC stimulation produces frequency and phase-dependent changes in Purkinje cell complex spike waveform.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Cerebellar transcranial alternating current stimulation (ctACS) can improve motor learning and may speed rehabilitation. The mechanisms by which ctACS induces long-term changes in brain function that underlie these effects are not known, and knowledge of them could greatly improve the application of ctACS. One potential mechanism is alteration of Purkinje cell (PC) complex spike (CS) activity, as CS activity is a key regulator of cerebellar synaptic plasticity. Thus, we investigated how ctACS modifies CS firing rates and waveform. Extracellular recordings were obtained from cerebellar PCs in anesthetized adult rats while ctACS (250 μA) was applied across a range of frequencies (0.5 - 50 Hz). The effect of ctACS on CS waveform was quantified via measuring changes in the overall size of the CS and in the number and amplitude of the spikelets that comprise a CS. ctACS produced phase‑dependent modulation of the CS waveform in a majority of PCs at most tested frequencies, with 1 Hz stimulation causing modulation in all PCs tested at the frequency. The modulation reflected changes within the normal range of CS waveforms rather than an expansion of that range. Analysis of individual spikelet periods (windows) revealed that ctACS modified discrete portions of the CS, with 93.8% of PCs showing significant modulation in at least one window. Notably, the strength of phase‑dependent CS waveform modulation was relatively consistent across frequencies, in contrast to the frequency dependence of simple spike (SS) entrainment. Significant modulation of spikelet amplitude was found more often than that of spikelet number; however, the relative strength of the modulation when present was similar for the two parameters. CS waveform modulation was correlated with SS entrainment strength and was strongest in PCs located near the cerebellar surface (i.e., near the apices of the folia). Together, these findings demonstrate that ctACS exerts phase‑dependent control over CS waveform. Moreover, the differing frequency dependence of the waveform effects and SS firing modulation suggests that it may be possible to target CS‑related plasticity selectively, providing a potential strategy for selectively modulating cerebellar learning with ctACS.

title: Topographic reference modelling of white matter hyperintensities across the adult lifespan.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are among the most common MRI findings in older adults. They are widely regarded as markers of brain aging and cerebral small-vessel disease, and associated with risk for cognitive decline, Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD), and stroke. White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are typically interpreted by total lesion burden, but lesions with similar volumes can occupy different anatomical locations, potentially reflecting distinct pathological processes. Here we present voxelwise topographic reference modelling (vTRM), a framework for characterizing individual WMH masks against age- and sex-stratified frequency maps derived from cognitively unimpaired individuals. Using 42,469 FLAIR-derived lesion masks from twelve adult cohorts, we mapped population-level WMH spatial vulnerability, characterized age-related changes in its distribution across periventricular, lobar and arterial-territory compartments, and constructed paired percentile charts for lesion burden and spatial typicality. A quadrant-based classification defined by these two percentile dimensions revealed graded relationships with ADRD pathophysiology, neurodegeneration, and cognitive impairment, while identifying WMH patterns differentially associated with ageing-related, vascular and neurodegenerative processes among individuals with similar lesion volumes. These reference charts establish a benchmark for normative WMH ageing, enabling quantification of individual deviations from typical age-, sex- and burden-related patterns and identification of WMH phenotypes associated with vascular, neurodegenerative or mixed etiologies. The framework, together with a deployable 3D U-Net model trained on these data for automated WMH segmentation, is available through the Brain Lesion Analytics platform ( https://brainlesionanalytics.org/ ).

title: Healthcare costs associated with lower respiratory tract infections among older adults in Sweden: a cost analysis.
abstract: Lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality globally, particularly among older adults. Despite their clinical significance, the long-term economic burden of LRTIs remains underexplored. To estimate healthcare costs associated with recorded LRTI exposure among Swedish adults aged ≥60 years. A deterministic cost calculator applied Swedish unit costs to aggregated healthcare resource utilization (HCRU) inputs from a previous longitudinal Swedish National Study of Aging and Care in Kungsholmen (SNAC-K) cohort study of 567 adults with recorded LRTI and 1,701 matched adults without recorded LRTI. Mean cumulative all-cause hospital days, hospital admissions and outpatient visits per participant were valued over 1, 3 and 5 years and up to 16 years. Results are presented primarily in euros (€), with Swedish kronor (SEK) also reported. At one year, estimated mean costs associated with subsequent all-cause hospital days were €39,112 (444,701 SEK) among LRTI-exposed participants and €14,712 (167,278 SEK) among unexposed participants, a descriptive absolute difference of €24,400 (277,423 SEK). Higher descriptive cost estimates were also observed among males and participants aged 60-74 years. Cost uncertainty was not quantified, and the results should not be interpreted as causal effects of LRTI. Recorded LRTI exposure was associated with higher descriptive cost estimates for several categories of subsequent all-cause HCRU among older adults in Sweden, with the largest displayed hospital-day cost difference during the first year. The findings provide descriptive economic context for healthcare planning; the effects and economic value of specific preventive strategies require separate evaluation.

title: Self-Rectifying ZnO/PZT Ferroelectric Synapses With Polarization-Modulated Transport for Read-Penalty-Resilient Neuromorphic Computing.
abstract: Sneak-path currents and readout penalties remain critical bottlenecks that limit the scalability and reliability of crossbar-array-based neuromorphic hardware. Here, we experimentally demonstrate self-rectifying Al/ZnO/Pb(Zr1-x,Tix)O3​(PZT)/Pt ferroelectric synapses with polarization-modulated transport and improved weight-update linearity and further evaluate their potential for read-penalty-aware neuromorphic computing through device-informed simulations. The ZnO/PZT heterostructure incorporates a ZnO transport layer that suppresses leakage during polarization switching in PZT while inducing pronounced self-rectifying and nonlinear current-voltage characteristics governed by space-charge-limited conduction. This enables gradual and stable multi-level conductance modulation via ferroelectric polarization-mediated memristive hysteresis behavior. Pulse-driven measurements confirm robust short- and long-term synaptic plasticity, and an amplitude-modulated pulse scheme significantly improves the linearity and symmetry of potentiation/depression updates with high cycle-to-cycle reproducibility. When incorporated into a neural network using experimentally extracted characteristics, the system achieves enhanced inference accuracy. More importantly, device-informed readout-penalty analysis indicates that the combination of improved update linearity and intrinsic rectification provides consistent gains in noise tolerance, read-failure robustness, and overall inference accuracy under the modeled readout conditions. These results establish polarization-modulated self-rectifying ferroelectric synapses as a promising device architecture for bridging device-level transport characteristics with projected readout robustness in neuromorphic systems.

title: Kinetic oscillation stimulation by the Chordate System S101 in the treatment of non-allergic rhinitis (KOSNAR): a randomised controlled trial.
journal: The Journal of laryngology and otology
abstract: To determine whether kinetic oscillation stimulation is superior to sham treatment for non-allergic rhinitis. In this multi-centre, double-blinded, sham-controlled trial, patients with non-allergic rhinitis received intranasal kinetic oscillation stimulation or placebo on two treatment occasions. The primary outcome was improvement in nasal congestion score at three months. Secondary outcomes included total nasal symptom score, nasal obstruction and septoplasty effectiveness score, EQ-5D-5L and peak nasal inspiratory flow. Of 279 recruited patients, 224 were analysed (112 patients received kinetic oscillation stimulation, 112 placebo). Response rates did not differ (40 per cent vs 46 per cent; p = 0.30). Both groups improved over time in total nasal symptom score (median change -2 vs -2; p = 0.81), nasal congestion score (-0.35 vs -1; p = 0.18) and nasal obstruction and septoplasty effectiveness score (-15 vs -15; p = 0.80), without significant between-group differences. Peak nasal inspiratory flow did not improve in the treatment group. This confirmatory trial found no superiority of kinetic oscillation stimulation over sham and does not support kinetic oscillation stimulation for non-allergic rhinitis.

title: [Ketamine-induced cystitis : an emerging condition].
abstract: Recreational ketamine use has risen sharply in recent years and can lead to dependance with a sixfold-increased risk of severe urinary tract symptoms among regular users. The resulting cystitis first affects the bladder wall, causing inflammation and fibrosis, before potentially extending to the upper urinary tract in advanced forms. A quarter of frequent users develop symptoms such as urinary frequency, pelvic pain or haematuria, which can progress to permanent damage without treatment. Work-up combines history, imaging and cystoscopy. Treatment begins with cessation, supplemented by pharmacological measures and, in refractory cases, reconstructive surgery. Prognosis depends mainly on how early the diagnosis is made and the patient's ability to sustain cessation.

title: Cannabidiol attenuates iron-associated oxidative neurotoxicity in the human and mouse prefrontal cortex following methamphetamine exposure.
abstract: Methamphetamine (METH) is a highly addictive psychostimulant, and its abuse results in severe neurotoxicity and drug addiction. However, the exact molecular mechanism through which METH causes this damage is incompletely understood. In the current study, we investigated whether ferroptosis-associated changes, an iron-dependent form of cell death involving lipid peroxidation and glutathione peroxidase-4 (GPX-4) depletion, contribute to METH-induced brain damage and whether cannabidiol (CBD) pretreatment exerts a neuroprotective effect. Post-mortem prefrontal cortex brain tissue from confirmed chronic METH users and matched controls was examined for ferroptosis biomarkers. In parallel, a mouse conditioned place preference (CPP) model was used to evaluate METH-induced behavioral effects and neurochemical changes with CBD pretreatment. METH users exhibited increased iron levels, higher levels of lipid peroxidation, lower GPX-4 expression, and elevated cell death compared with control individuals. Similarly, mice repeatedly exposed to METH developed a strong place preference and exhibited increased iron levels, higher lipid peroxidation, lower GPX-4 expression, and elevated cell death. While CBD pretreatment significantly reduced the behavioral and biochemical changes induced by METH. Our findings show that chronic METH exposure induces iron-associated oxidative neurotoxicity in the prefrontal cortex, with changes consistent with ferroptosis-like cell damage, and that CBD pretreatment partially reduces these effects. This suggests that CBD has a potential preventive neuroprotective effect against METH-induced oxidative damage.

title: Docosahexaenoic acid and Alzheimer's disease: a systematic review.
abstract: Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), an omega-3 fatty acid found in marine sources, has gained attention for its potential therapeutic role in Alzheimer's disease (AD). This review systematically examines evidence from clinical studies and preclinical models regarding the potential of DHA to enhance cognitive function and protect against neurodegeneration linked to AD. DHA modulates inflammatory pathways, potentially reducing neuroinflammation associated with AD, and its antioxidant properties may help mitigate oxidative stress, a critical factor in neuronal degeneration. DHA has been reported to reduce neuroinflammatory mediators, enhance antioxidant enzyme activity, and stabilize neuronal membrane fluidity. It promotes synaptic plasticity through the upregulation of NMDA receptor subunits (NR2A/NR2B), tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), synaptophysin, and postsynaptic density protein-95 (PSD-95), and enhances neurogenesis in the dentate gyrus. DHA has been associated with improvements in learning, memory performance, and various markers of neuronal function. However, variability across studies - including differences in DHA source, dosage, duration, and study design - affects the consistency of observed outcomes. DHA may exert multiple neuroprotective actions relevant to AD, including anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, membrane-modulating, and synaptic-supportive effects. These mechanisms may contribute to improvements in cognitive and neuronal outcomes. Combining DHA with other therapeutic agents - antioxidants and anti-inflammatory drugs - represents a potential approach to AD treatment.

title: Terminology in "epilepsy surgery".
The association of childhood maltreatment, depression, and their combination with adiposity and dyslipidemia: an individual participant data meta-analysis.
authors: Mulders Annemarie G M G J
Van Der Wee Nic J A
abstract: While childhood maltreatment and depression are recognized risk factors for poor metabolic health, the extent to which these individually or in combination with each other contribute to metabolic risk remains unknown. Therefore, we investigated adiposity and dyslipidemia across four groups: adults with neither a history of childhood maltreatment nor depression (controls), with childhood maltreatment, with depression, or with both. We conducted an individual participant data meta-analysis using 11 cohort studies. Childhood maltreatment was assessed with reports of physical, emotional, and/or sexual abuse. Depression was established with clinical interviews or validated symptom scales. Adiposity was assessed with body mass index (BMI) and waist-to-hip ratio (WHR) and dyslipidemia with circulating triglycerides and low-density/high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio (LDL-c/HDL-c). In the pooled sample (N = 167,332), 6% had childhood maltreatment, 21% depression, and 6% both. Compared to controls, participants with maltreatment had slightly higher adiposity (dBMI=0.06 [95%CI, 0.01-0.10], p=.012; dWHR=0.06 [95%CI, 0.01-0.12], p=.030) but similar lipid levels (dtriglycerides=0.01 [95%CI, ‒0.03-0.04], p=.751; dLDL-c/HDL-c=0.01 [95%CI, ‒0.03-0.06], p=.560). Those with depression had higher adiposity (dBMI=0.06 [95%CI, 0.01-0.12], p=.030; dWHR=0.12 [95%CI, 0.08-0.16], p<.001) and dyslipidemia (dtriglycerides=0.08 [95%CI, 0.04-0.12], p<.001; dLDL-c/HDL-c=0.13 [95%CI, 0.07-0.18], p<.001). Participants with both maltreatment and depression had the highest adiposity (dBMI=0.17 [95%CI, 0.04-0.30], p=.010; dWHR=0.16 [95%CI, 0.07-0.24], p<.001) and dyslipidemia (dtriglycerides=0.14 [95%CI, 0.11-0.16], p<.001; dLDL-c/HDL-c=0.18 [95%CI, 0.12-0.23], p<.001).
