Childhood maltreatment and depression are associated with unfavorable metabolic health, with the largest dysregulations found when maltreatment and depression co-occur. Mechanisms of metabolic dysregulation in maltreatment and/or depression should be better understood to prevent progression to metabolic disorders.

title: Response to: "Paroxysmal slow waves and deep temporal discharges: Revisiting Chatrian and Gastaut".
Detection of Impulse Control Behaviors in Parkinson's Disease: Incremental Yield of Unstructured Psychiatric Interviews over QUIP Screening and Routine Clinical Assessment.
abstract: Impulse control behaviors (ICBs) are common but under-recognized non-motor complications of Parkinson's disease (PD), arising from dopaminergic overstimulation of fronto-striatal reward circuits. Self-report tools such as the Questionnaire for Impulsive-Compulsive Disorders in PD (QUIP) are limited by reduced insight, recall bias and reluctance to disclose sensitive behaviors. To compare approaches to ICB detection in PD-outpatient referral documentation, QUIP screening, and a clinician-led unstructured psychiatric interview (UPI) integrating informant testimony-and to characterize the spectrum and co-occurrence of ICB subtypes. In this prospective observational single-center study, 144 inpatients with idiopathic PD were evaluated at admission to a neuropsychiatric unit by these approaches. Detection rates were compared using McNemar's test. ICBs were identified in 13.2% via referral data, 20.8% via QUIP and 36.1% via UPI (McNemar p < 0.001). UPI yielded a 15.3-percentage-point increment over QUIP, including detection of reckless generosity (not represented in QUIP) and clinically relevant presentations of dopamine dysregulation syndrome and punding that were under-detected by screening items. Co-occurring ICBs were common: 27.8% of patients exhibited two or more subtypes, 14.6% four or more, and 2.1% up to seven. In a subgroup analysis, patients with ≥6 ICBs (n = 7) were uniformly male, dopamine agonist-treated, younger and had longer disease duration. Routine clinical assessment and self-report screening substantially underestimate the prevalence and complexity of ICBs in PD. A comprehensive informant-supported psychiatric interview improves detection and reveals clinically relevant phenotypic clustering, with implications for dopaminergic therapy adjustment and pre-DBS evaluation.

title: Cannabis use and mental health symptoms in adolescents and adults: a 4-year longitudinal study.
abstract: Adolescence may be characterised by increased sensitivity to the psychological harms of chronic cannabis use. However, few studies have directly compared the consequences of cannabis use on adolescent and adult mental health over time. We ran a 4-year longitudinal study of 274 participants, who were recruited as mid-adolescents (16-17 years) and young adults (26-29 years). At baseline, participants either used cannabis (≥1 day/week) or did not. We measured drug use, mental health, and cognitive function every 3 months for 1 year and ~4 years post-baseline. We ran linear mixed models to estimate associations between time-varying cannabis use frequency and our outcomes. We covaried for sociodemographic, environmental, and polygenic risk variables. Adolescents were more likely to have problematic cannabis use symptoms than adults (p = .001). Cannabis use frequency was associated with: severity of problematic cannabis use (p < .001), psychotic-like symptoms (p = .003), and worse spatial working memory performance (p = .038). Cannabis use cessation was associated with reductions in psychotic-like (p = .005) and depressive symptoms (p = .016). Most cannabis use by age-group interactions were null. Adolescents have a persistently enhanced risk of problematic cannabis use. Using cannabis more frequently is associated with greater psychotic-like symptoms and worse spatial working memory. Apart from problematic cannabis use, we found no significant evidence that mid-to-late adolescents are especially vulnerable to the associations between cannabis use and poorer mental health. However, cessation of cannabis use was linked to improvements in mental health.

title: Paroxysmal slow waves and deep temporal discharges: Revisiting Chatrian and Gastaut.
Neurocognitive deficits in controlling aversive memory in insomnia disorder.
abstract: Insomnia disorder is a common sleep disturbance characterized by cognitive hyperarousal, such as intrusive and uncontrollable thoughts (e.g. thoughts about sleeplessness, worries). Memory control, a key self-regulatory ability to control or inhibit unwanted thoughts and memories, plays an essential role in supporting cognitive functions and emotional well-being. Here, we delineate the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying memory control among individuals with insomnia. Forty-one participants meeting DSM-5 criteria for insomnia disorder and 40 healthy sleepers completed an emotional Think/No-Think task, during which they were instructed to either retrieve (Think), suppress the retrieval (No-Think) of aversive memories, or visually process cues without retrieval or suppress retrieval (Perceptual Baseline). At the same time, electroencephalographic (EEG) activity was recorded. Linear mixed model analyses with age and depression scores as covariates showed that the insomnia group exhibited impaired memory control abilities, as evidenced by reduced suppression-induced forgetting during memory recall compared with the healthy group. Electrophysiologically, the insomnia group showed enhanced P300, a well-established neural marker of conscious episodic retrieval, in the No-Think condition compared to the Perceptual Baseline condition, indicating residual episodic retrieval during memory suppression. In contrast, this difference was absent among the healthy group, suggesting successful inhibition or abolishment of the memory traces. Individuals with insomnia showed impaired memory control of aversive memories and aberrant electrophysiological activities during retrieval suppression. Future research shall investigate the neural mechanisms underlying memory control deficits in insomnia disorder and the causal relationship between memory control abilities and insomnia symptoms.

title: Mitochondrial dysfunction at the crossroads of liver disease and depression: Focus on the liver-brain axis.
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction may provide a biological link between liver disease and major depressive disorder (MDD), two conditions that frequently coexist. In chronic liver disease, changes in energy metabolism, redox balance, Ca2+ homeostasis, and mitochondrial quality control promote metabolic stress, inflammation, and tissue injury. Studies of MDD report related mitochondrial changes that affect neuronal activity, neuroinflammation, and synaptic function. The liver and brain also exchange metabolic and inflammatory signals through the circulation, autonomic nerves, and the gut. Recent studies have identified hepatic acetate metabolism, complement component 3, lipocalin 2, and hepatic clearance of neuroactive microbial metabolites as components of this communication. Vagal and sympathetic pathways provide additional routes, while liver injury can also alter mitochondrial function in the brain. In this review, we integrate clinical and experimental evidence to examine how these processes may contribute to the comorbidity of liver disease and depression. We also discuss the limits of current evidence and consider how spatial and single-cell profiling, brain bioenergetic imaging, and liver-directed interventions can test the proposed mechanisms. Together, current evidence supports mitochondrial dysfunction as a plausible and testable link between hepatic and neural pathology and provides a framework for studying liver disease and depression comorbidity.

title: Data-driven classification for avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder.
abstract: ARFID is a heterogeneous illness characterized by restrictive eating secondary to sensory sensitivity, lack of interest in eating or food, and/or a fear of aversive consequences. Research utilizing data-driven approaches to examine the nosology of ARFID is scant, but needed to inform etiological inquiry and treatment planning. We aimed to examine whether a hybrid categorical-dimensional model of ARFID could explain within-ARFID heterogeneity. We used Pica, ARFID, and Rumination Disorder Interview (PARDI) data from 188 children, adolescents, and adults to fit a Gaussian finite mixture model (GFMM) to inform the nosology of ARFID. The data were collected from three separate National Institute of Mental Health-funded studies. The best-fitting GFMM identified four classes, indicating that ARFID symptom distribution varied across the groups. We labeled the groups: Mild Interest-Sensory Phenotype (n = 115, 61%), Mild Three Phenotype (n = 30, 16%), Moderate-to-High Three Phenotype (n = 27, 14%), and High Fear-Interest/Mild Sensory Phenotype (n = 16, 9%). Validation analyses supported significant differences among the GFMM-identified groups, such that the Moderate-to-High Three Phenotype and High Fear-Interest/Mild Sensory Phenotype groups were more severe compared to the Mild Interest-Sensory Phenotype and the Mild Three Phenotype groups. Finally, results supported the dimensionality of sensory sensitivity and lack of interest and found that fear of aversive consequences may be more categorical. Our results found support for a hybrid categorical-dimensional model of ARFID and provided a new exploratory framework that could guide future etiological and treatment research efforts.

title: Childhood trauma and side-effects of antipsychotic medication after first-episode psychosis: A HAMLETT study.
abstract: Childhood trauma is a well-established risk factor for psychosis and is linked to worse outcomes and higher doses of antipsychotic medication needed. Trauma-exposed individuals also exhibit endocrinological, immunological, and metabolic alterations that may influence medication metabolism and sensitivity to side effects. This study examined whether childhood trauma severity predicts side-effect burden in individuals with first episode psychosis (FEP). This analysis utilized baseline data from the HAMLETT study. Participants in symptomatic remission following an FEP and receiving antipsychotics were included if they had completed the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire - Short Form (CTQ-SF), Subjective Reaction to Antipsychotics (SRA), Subjective Well-Being under Neuroleptics (SWN), and medication data (N = 235). Generalized linear regressions were conducted to examine associations between childhood trauma severity and side-effect outcomes. Models were adjusted for age, sex at birth, medication dose, and receptor profile. Moderation analysis was performed to assess whether sex influenced these associations. Childhood trauma severity was associated with more antipsychotic side effects, as assessed by both SWN (p < .001) and SRA (p = .001), independent of antipsychotic dose. The effect was also significant across all five SWN subscales and four out of seven SRA side-effect domains, namely, sedation, affective flattening, extrapyramidal symptoms, and diminished sociability. Moderation analyses showed no sex differences in SRA or SWN side-effect scores. Childhood trauma may be related to more side effects of antipsychotics experienced in individuals with FEP, independent of sex. Clinicians could expect a greater burden of side effects in individuals with childhood trauma and be extra alert for these effects.

title: Acute Ischemic Stroke Cases with a Rare Etiology: Free-Floating Thrombus (FFT); Experiences of a Single Centre.
abstract: Free-floating thrombus (FFT) is a rare and clinically critical imaging finding in acute ischemic stroke associated with a high embolic risk. This study aimed to evaluate the clinical, radiological, etiological, and therapeutic characteristics, as well as outcomes, of patients presenting with acute ischemic stroke and FFT. This retrospective single-center series included patients evaluated for acute ischemic stroke between 2021 and 2025 who met the study's FFT criteria on vascular imaging. Diagnosis used dynamic Doppler confirmation in accessible extracranial arteries and computed tomography angiography (CTA) morphology in anatomically inaccessible segments. Clinical presentation, etiology according to the Trial of Org 10172 in Acute Stroke Treatment (TOAST) classification, antithrombotic treatment, vascular outcomes, and 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) scores were described. Clinical and imaging follow-up extended to at least 6 months in surviving patients. Among 2150 patients with comprehensive vascular imaging, 31 (1.4%) met the FFT criteria (mean age, 61.4 ± 16.0 years; 54.8% female). The internal carotid artery was the most frequent location (25/31; 80.6%). TOAST categories were undetermined etiology in 17 patients (54.8%), cardioembolism in seven (22.6%), large-artery atherosclerosis in five (16.1%), and other determined etiologies in two (6.5%). The undetermined group comprised 15 patients without an identified cause and two with competing mechanisms. All patients initially received anticoagulation. Complete and partial recanalization were observed in 17 (54.8%) and 12 (38.7%) patients, respectively. Seven patients underwent carotid revascularization after thrombus stabilization, with no residual stenosis and no procedure-related complications within 30 days. At 90 days, 28 patients (90.3%) had mRS scores of 0-2. FFT is a morphological finding occurring across different stroke mechanisms. This series describes imaging-based assessment, initial anticoagulation, and subsequent carotid revascularization in selected patients. Its uncontrolled, descriptive design does not establish treatment efficacy, an optimal anticoagulation duration, or the preferred timing of intervention.

title: Allosteric modulation of GluN2B-containing glutamate receptors reduces seizures in autoimmune encephalitis.
abstract: Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (anti-NMDAR) encephalitis manifests with encephalopathy, seizures, cognitive impairment, and sleep disruption that respond poorly to conventional therapies; novel effective treatments are urgently needed. GluN2B-containing NMDARs play important roles in seizure generation and cognition; however, their contribution to anti-NMDAR encephalitis remains unclear. We investigated whether patient-derived anti-NMDAR antibodies alter synaptic GluN1 and GluN2B receptor expression and whether selective GluN2B inhibition affects seizures, memory, and sleep in a mouse model of anti-NMDAR encephalitis. Male C57BL/6 mice (8-12 weeks old, n = 9-11 per group) were continuously infused for 14 days with monoclonal anti-NMDAR antibodies derived from a patient with anti-NMDAR encephalitis or with control IgG. Seizures and sleep were monitored using continuous electroencephalographic recordings. Traxoprodil (10 mg/kg i.p., daily), a selective negative allosteric modulator of GluN2B, was administered throughout the infusion period. Locomotor activity, anxiety-like behavior, and memory were assessed using open field and object location paradigms. Synaptosomes were isolated from whole brain tissue and were processed for GluN1 and GluN2B protein expression by Western blot. Consistent with prior studies, 89% of anti-NMDAR antibody-exposed mice developed seizures, with a median of 8 seizures over 2 weeks (interquartile range = 3-18). Antibody-infused mice also demonstrated hippocampus-dependent memory impairment and reduced rapid eye movement (REM) sleep compared to control mice. Traxoprodil diminished seizures (p = .02) but did not alter memory and sleep dysfunction. Anti-NMDAR IgG exposure markedly reduced synaptic GluN1 and GluN2B protein expression, and traxoprodil prevented this (p = .0002 and p = .02, respectively). Our study demonstrates sleep disruption in an animal model of anti-NMDAR encephalitis and highlights the selective role of GluN2B signaling in seizure expression. The persistence of cognitive and sleep disruption during traxoprodil treatment suggests distinct pathophysiological mechanisms. Selective modulation of GluN2B may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for seizure management in anti-NMDAR encephalitis.

title: Association of Feeding Therapy Timing and Frequency With Time to Independent Oral Feeding in Infants With Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy.
abstract: To characterize feeding therapy utilization and delivery patterns and examine associations of therapy dose (timing and frequency) with time to independent oral feeding in infants with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE). We conducted a retrospective cohort study of infants with HIE treated with therapeutic hypothermia and discharged feeding independently by mouth from two Level IV neonatal intensive care unit (NICUs) between 2017 and 2024. Multivariable linear regression assessed associations of therapy timing and frequency with time to independent oral feeding, adjusting for encephalopathy severity, abnormality on brain magnetic resonance imaging, and intubation days. Among 358 infants, 326 (91%) received feeding therapy. Therapy was initiated a median of 1.5 d after therapeutic hypothermia and was delivered at a median of 3.5 sessions per week. Each day of delayed initiation was associated with a 0.5 d longer time to independent oral feeding (95% CI 0.3-0.7), and each additional weekly session with a 1 d shorter time to independent oral feeding (95% CI: -1.5 to -0.5). Earlier initiation and greater frequency of feeding therapy were associated with faster attainment of independent oral feeding. Therapy timing and frequency may represent potentially modifiable aspects of NICU care that warrant prospective investigation.

title: A Randomized Controlled Clinical Study on the Efficacy of Tiaoren Tongdu Acupuncture in Older Adults With Mild-to-Moderate Depression.
abstract: This study aimed to assess the clinical efficacy of the Tiaoren Tongdu acupuncture method in older adults diagnosed with mild-to-moderate depressive disorder. A total of 80 patients with mild-to-moderate depressive disorder, randomly assigned using a random number table to a control group (n = 40) or an intervention group (n = 40), were included in the analysis. Participants in the control group received conventional acupuncture treatment, whereas those in the intervention group received the Tiaoren Tongdu acupuncture protocol. Both interventions were administered once daily, with six sessions constituting one treatment course and a total of six treatment courses completed over a 6-week period. The primary outcome was the 24-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD-24); secondary outcomes included the Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS-30), the Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS), and serum levels of 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT), norepinephrine (NE), and dopamine (DA). All outcomes were assessed at baseline and following treatment. Following treatment, HAMD-24 and SAS scores were significantly reduced compared with baseline in both groups, whereas GDS-30 scores were significantly reduced in the intervention group but not in the control group, with significantly lower HAMD-24 and GDS-30 scores observed in the intervention group than in the control group (p < 0.0001), and a significantly lower SAS score (p < 0.05), with a median between-group difference of one point (median 53.00 vs. 54.00). In addition, serum concentrations of 5-HT, NE, and DA increased significantly from baseline in both groups (p < 0.0001), with significantly higher post-treatment levels in the intervention group compared with the control group (p < 0.0001). The Tiaoren Tongdu acupuncture method was associated with improvements in depressive and anxiety symptom severity, as well as increased monoamine neurotransmitter levels, in older adults with mild-to-moderate depressive disorder, demonstrating an acceptable safety profile. ITMCTR registration number: ITMCTR2026000972.

title: The Clinical Connectome in EBRAINS 2.0.
abstract: Neurological diseases, including stroke, Parkinson's disease (PD), and gliomas, have traditionally been interpreted through a focal-based lens, where symptoms are primarily attributed to the location and extent of neural damage. Converging evidence has reframed these conditions as circuitopathies, in which the disruption of brain networks underlies clinical manifestations. Yet, a network-integrated approach remains far from routine clinical practice. The aggregation of large datasets, which enables testing hypotheses about diagnosis, prognosis, or response to therapy across independent cohorts as well as prediction at the level of individual patients, is a critical step toward closing this translational gap. We describe the Clinical Connectome initiative developed within Work Package 2 of the EBRAINS 2.0 project, a translational effort that aims to bridge network neuroscience and clinical neurology. We first review stroke, PD, and gliomas as complementary models of brain network disruption, highlighting how the different pathophysiological mechanisms converge on shared patterns of network perturbation. We then present the Platform for Human Imaging, a GDPR-compliant infrastructure that enables secure storage, harmonized processing, and controlled dissemination of multimodal neuroimaging and clinical data across European institutions. To date, the Clinical Connectome has aggregated data from over 7000 patients across institutions. A Delphi consensus panel, conducted in collaboration with the European Academy of Neurology (EAN), has established harmonized protocols for the prospective data acquisition in these disorders. By providing an integrated framework linking clinical neuroimaging to brain atlases and computational modeling, the Clinical Connectome aims to lay the foundations for network-based precision neurology.

title: Gsx1 modulates endogenous progenitors to promote excitatory circuit remodeling following spinal cord injury.
journal: Molecular therapy : the journal of the American Society of Gene Therapy
abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) activates endogenous neural stem and progenitor cells (NSPCs), yet their response is largely restricted to gliogenesis and insufficient for effective circuit repair. The homeobox transcription factor Gsx1 regulates excitatory interneuron specification during development, but its ability to reengage endogenous repair programs in the adult injured spinal cord remains unclear. Here, we show that AAV6-mediated Gsx1 expression promotes functional recovery after contusion SCI by linking acute progenitor state remodeling with chronic excitatory circuit reorganization. Gsx1 treatment significantly improved locomotor coordination and mechanical sensory recovery. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis during the acute phase revealed that Gsx1 shifts ependymal cells toward naïve and stem-like states and biases oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs) away from proliferative programs toward myelinating and synaptogenic phenotypes. During the chronic phase, single-nucleus transcriptomics and histological analyses demonstrated a shift in neuronal composition toward excitatory interneuron identities, with pronounced enrichment of Chx10/Vsx2+ glutamatergic interneurons, enhanced synaptogenesis-related signaling, and increased neuronal activity. Mechanistically, Ascl1 knockdown in OPC-lineage cells attenuated early OPC responses, reduced chronic excitatory interneuron enrichment, and diminished Gsx1-mediated locomotor recovery. Together, these findings identify Gsx1 as a regulator of endogenous NSPC plasticity that redeploys developmental excitatory patterning programs to promote circuit remodeling and functional recovery after SCI.

title: A minimal physical model of adhesion-dependent protrusion explains confined haptotaxis and oscillatory cell migration.
abstract: Haptotaxis is the directed migration of cells along gradients of substrate adhesion, and is an important guidance mechanism in biology. Recent experiments on fibronectin-patterned tracks show that cells typically migrate toward higher adhesion, then oscillate around the adhesion maximum, with substantial variability in speed and cell length. To explain these cellular shape and migration dynamics we present a minimal model for confined haptotaxis, built around one key physical ingredient: local adhesion strength directly enhances the recruitment of protrusive actin polymerization activity at the cell edge. This coupling creates a front-rear difference in protrusive activity, biasing the cell towards polarization in the direction of the higher adhesion. Quantitative comparison with experiment shows strong agreement at multiple levels: cell population-level directionality statistics and position-dependent changes in cell length and velocity. At the single-cell level, the model reproduces the full diversity of experimentally observed trajectories, including haptotactic bias and its dependence on adhesion-gradient strength, initial position, length and speed variations, myosin II inhibition, and migration on inverted adhesion gradients. Variability in experimental trajectories and migration speed is explained by differences in intrinsic actin polymerization activity and stochastic fluctuations, accounting for the full spectrum of observed migration patterns. Together, our results identify adhesion-dependent amplification of protrusive activity as a minimal and sufficient physical mechanism for understanding haptotaxis.

title: Evaluation of the M444/Solanidine Metabolic Ratio for CYP2D6 Activity Assessment: Comparison With Dextromethorphan Phenotyping.
abstract: Interindividual variability in drug response is largely influenced by CYP2D6, which determines the metabolism of 20% of marketed drugs. CYP2D6 is currently assessed by genotyping or drug phenotyping, through costly and specialized methods. Solanidine, a potato-derived alkaloid metabolized by CYP2D6 into several metabolites, including M444, is a promising endogenous biomarker reflecting real-time CYP2D6 activity, capturing both genetic and environmental factors. The objective of this study is to evaluate whether the plasma solanidine metabolic ratio (M444/solanidine) can serve as a surrogate marker of CYP2D6 activity by comparison with the reference dextromethorphan metabolic ratio. In this retrospective study, solanidine and M444 were semiquantified by LC-MS/MS in 69 patients previously phenotyped to optimize analgesic or psychotropic therapy. Eleven patients were excluded because solanidine and M444 were below the limit of detection, leaving 58 patients to analysis. The solanidine metabolic ratio strongly correlated with the dextromethorphan metabolic ratio (dextrorphan/dextromethorphan) (r = 0.67; p < 0.0001). It differed across CYP2D6 phenotype groups (p < 0.0001) and discriminated poor metabolizers (PM) from other phenotypes. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis for the identification of CYP2D6 PM yielded an area under the curve of 0.992, with an optimal metabolic ratio cut-off of 0.04 (Youden index: 0.98), corresponding to 100% sensitivity and 97.9% specificity. Although validation in larger studies, particularly under controlled potato intake, is needed, this study provides the first evidence in French patients that the solanidine metabolic ratio is a promising biomarker for identifying CYP2D6 PM and could support large-scale, cost-effective phenotyping for personalized medicine.

title: Microstructural MRI characteristics of white matter lesions are associated with clinical disability and retinal layer thicknesses in people with multiple sclerosis.
abstract: Quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (qMRI) captures central nervous system microstructural integrity aspects in people with multiple sclerosis (PwMS). To evaluate associations between white matter lesion (WML) qMRI measures, clinical disability, and retinal layer thicknesses in PwMS, and whether these differ between people with progressive (PwPMS) and relapsing MS (PwRMS). This prospective cross-sectional study included 125 participants who underwent 3T brain MRIs to estimate longitudinal relaxation time (T1), intrinsic (R2) and effective (R2*) transverse relaxation rates, microscopic fractional anisotropy (µFA), and paramagnetic/diamagnetic susceptibilities. Optical coherence tomography measured peri-papillary retinal nerve fiber layer (pRNFL) and ganglion cell-inner plexiform layer (GCIPL) thicknesses. Higher WML T1 was associated with greater Expanded Disability Status Scale (standardized β = 0.17, p = 0.04) and lower Symbol Digit Modalities Test (β = -0.29, p = 0.02) scores, as well as lower pRNFL (β = -0.26, p < 0.001) and GCIPL (β = -0.23, p = 0.003) thicknesses. Lower WML R2 and R2* were associated with lower pRNFL thicknesses. PwPMS had lower µFA than PwRMS (p = 0.02). WML qMRI measures, especially T1, are associated with disability and/or retinal layer thicknesses, linking WML microstructure (axonal degeneration/demyelination) to functional/structural outcomes in PwMS. WML microstructural damage appears more pronounced in PwPMS than PwRMS.

title: The Interplay of Cultural Beliefs, Emotional Distress, and Psychosocial Adjustment Among Cancer Survivors: A Mixed-Methods Study of Resilience.
abstract: Cultural beliefs may shape emotional well-being and psychosocial adjustment among cancer survivors, yet evidence on their interplay with emotional distress and resilience in sub-Saharan Africa remains limited. This study examined relationships among cultural beliefs, emotional distress, resilience, and psychosocial adjustment and explored the indirect role of resilience and the moderating role of cultural beliefs. A concurrent mixed-methods study was conducted at two public referral hospitals in Tanzania. Quantitative data from 381 cancer survivors were analyzed using hierarchical multiple regression and PROCESS Model 14, adjusting for demographic and clinical covariates. Semi-structured interviews with 20 survivors were analyzed thematically. After adjustment, emotional distress was negatively (β = -0.342, p < 0.001) and cultural beliefs positively (β = 0.365, p < 0.001) associated with psychosocial adjustment. Resilience partially mediated the association between emotional distress and psychosocial adjustment, with significant indirect effects at all levels of cultural beliefs. However, cultural beliefs did not significantly moderate the association between resilience and adjustment. Qualitative findings showed that cultural beliefs could both hinder adjustment through stigma and treatment-related conflicts and support resilience through spirituality, family, and community resources, which may explain the absence of statistical moderation. Emotional distress and cultural beliefs were independently associated with psychosocial adjustment, and resilience partly accounted for the distress-adjustment association. Cultural beliefs acted as both a resource and a risk rather than a consistent moderator. Culturally responsive survivorship care should address distress and stigma while strengthening resilience and supportive cultural, spiritual, family, and community resources.

title: The serotonin-endocannabinoid tango.
abstract: The serotonergic and endocannabinoid (eCB) systems constitute two principal neuromodulatory axes that regulate mood, cognition, stress responses, and synaptic plasticity. Although historically examined as independent entities, a growing body of evidence demonstrates sophisticated bidirectional crosstalk between these systems at multiple levels of organization. This crosstalk is facilitated by extensive co-expression of CB1 receptors with various 5-HTR subtypes in brain regions, including the dorsal raphe nucleus, hippocampus, amygdala, and prefrontal cortex. Functionally, eCBs modulate serotonergic neuron activity via presynaptic CB1 receptors located on glutamatergic, GABAergic, and serotonergic terminals. Conversely, serotonin reciprocally mobilizes eCB synthesis through postsynaptic 5-HT2A receptor activation. This review summarizes our current knowledge on five key aspects: (1) the fundamental properties of each system, (2) anatomical substrates enabling their interaction, (3) eCB-mediated control of serotonin release, (4) serotonin-induced eCB synthesis, and (5) the impact of depression on this bidirectional interaction.

title: Longitudinal plasma p-tau217 and proteomic correlates of lecanemab pharmacodynamic response in a real-world Chinese Alzheimer's disease cohort.
journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association
abstract: Early biological responses to lecanemab vary among patients, but blood-based pharmacodynamic correlates remain incompletely characterized. We analyzed 119 patients over 28 weeks. Plasma biomarkers were measured serially; 58 patients had paired amyloid positron emission tomography (PET), 85 baseline proteomics, and 62 paired proteomics. Longitudinal phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) trajectories defined pharmacodynamic response strata. P-tau217 declined by 14.6% and 26.6% at Weeks 14 and 28, respectively, and its change was associated with standardized uptake value ratio reduction (false discovery rate [FDR] = 0.014). High-response participants showed greater PET reduction; cognitive group-by-time interactions were not statistically significant. Baseline proteomics identified 317 proteins meeting joint FDR/effect-size criteria and response-associated modules. Paired proteomics showed complement and humoral immune pathway enrichment. In an exploratory analysis, amyloid-related imaging abnormalities were more frequent in the high-response group (27.3% vs 9.3%; adjusted odds ratio = 2.81; 95% CI: 1.03 to 8.09). Longitudinal p-tau217 reflected early pharmacodynamic heterogeneity, whereas plasma proteomics identified candidate molecular correlates of response.

title: Mitochondrial dynamics regulation in neurogenesis during cerebral ischemia-reperfusion.
abstract: Ischemic stroke ranks among the leading causes of death and disability worldwide. Vascular recanalization after stroke can trigger cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury(CIRI), which disturbs mitochondrial homeostasis and blunts endogenous neurogenesis, limiting brain functional recovery. Although mitochondrial dynamics govern neural stem cell fate under physiological conditions, how this machinery reshapes neurogenesis specifically in the pathological context of CIRI remains incompletely synthesized. This review focuses on the mechanistic links between mitochondrial dynamics disturbance, impaired energy metabolism, and defective endogenous neurogenesis under CIRI, as well as therapeutic strategies targeting mitochondrial dynamics to restore neurogenesis after reperfusion insult. Relevant literature on neurogenesis, energy metabolism, and mitochondrial dynamics was reviewed to elucidate their roles in CIRI. Additionally, experimental data on mitochondrial dynamics-related proteins regulating neurogenesis were examined, with special attention to findings obtained from cerebral ischemia-reperfusion experimental models. Therapeutic approaches promoting endogenous neurogenesis represent a novel strategy for treating ischemic-induced neural injury. Neurogenesis is closely linked to mitochondrial energy metabolism. In CIRI, reperfusion stress disrupts the balance of mitochondrial fission-fusion, which further impairs metabolic reprogramming required for neural stem cell activation, proliferation and neuronal survival. Direct in-vivo evidence connecting mitochondrial dynamics remodeling to neurogenesis in CIRI is still limited. Targeting mitochondrial dynamics to rescue energy homeostasis may serve as a means to revive endogenous neurogenesis post-CIRI. Energy metabolism and pathological changes following cerebral ischemia-reperfusion are closely associated with mitochondrial dynamics. Modulating mitochondrial dynamics holds potential to rescue metabolic disturbance and restore neurogenesis after CIRI.
